reconcile-deposit-holds — the sweep that resolves stale pending ledger links against Stripe
Customer-initiated early settlement: pay one installment now, or pay off every remaining installment at once
Recover the saved card from the Stripe customer when the plan stored no payment_method_id, and backfill it onto the plan
Ledger allocation performed inline (payment entry, charge remaining_amount, payment_applications) rather than by calling apply-payment over HTTP
Installments are flipped to 'processing' before Stripe and reverted to 'scheduled' with a failure reason when the charge fails
Pay-off charges ONE PaymentIntent for the summed remainder, marks every slot paid, and closes the plan as completed
Every payment row is stamped with the platform_account the charge was created on (getChargePlatformAccount)
Place a security-deposit authorisation on the renter's saved card as a manual-capture PaymentIntent (authorize only, never charge)
Ask Stripe whether the recorded hold is still alive before refusing — a DB 'held' is not proof of a live authorisation
Only canceled / succeeded / requires_payment_method conclusively mean the authorisation is dead; anything still in motion is treated as alive so a card is never authorised twice
The dead-status map is duplicated in create-hold-checkout because _shared/stripe-client.ts is owned by another workstream and this guard pair had to ship without touching it

GMT incident, Aug 2026: rentals.deposit_hold_status is written once and never revisited, so an expired authorisation still reads 'held' and every placement path short-circuits — 'I cannot refresh the hold'
Configured authorisation for the widest caller set of the deposit family: service-role webhooks, portal staff, the signed-in renter, and unidentified guest-booking automation

Guest bookings are admitted with no session at all for AUTOMATIC placement only — the webhook path needs metadata only the portal sets, so refusing would silently stop deposits on every customer-originated booking
A proven human identity always wins over a client-supplied actor when writing the deposit_hold_links ledger, so nobody can sign another person's name to a card authorisation
Two-tier extension guard: auto-extend rentals never get a hold from any caller; manually-extended rentals are blocked only for AUTOMATIC callers, and deliberate staff action passes manualOverride
A stale 'held' row is corrected to the truth before the claim, anchored to the exact status AND PaymentIntent probed, because the refresh cron can swap in a brand-new live PI under the same status
Yield to rows owned by another worker ('processing') or by the refresh cron ('refreshing') so the claim can never take a slot mid-flight and duplicate the authorisation
A numeric per-rental deposit override always wins, INCLUDING an explicit 0 meaning the operator opted out; only NULL falls back to the tenant default
per_vehicle deposit mode reads vehicles.security_deposit, hard-scoped to GMT's tenant id because the other per_vehicle tenants have a $0 global and would start collecting holds they do not take today
deposit_source and the full estimate_inputs are recorded on the ledger row so 'why was THIS amount authorised?' is answerable months later
Atomic compare-and-set claim of the hold slot which also MINTS deposit_hold_attempt_seq — only one caller can win, so only one caller can mint the attempt number
The Stripe idempotency key is keyed on the ATTEMPT, not the rental and not the dead PaymentIntent — both earlier schemes replayed a cached decline into a fresh attempt
Releasing the 'processing' claim is the recovery-critical write of every failure path: it runs first, retries once, and can never throw
The deposit_hold_links row is written BEFORE Stripe is contacted, so a crashed or timed-out attempt still leaves a discoverable trace of a possible orphan authorisation
supabase-js RESOLVES with {error} on a Postgres error but REJECTS on a transport failure, so both must be caught around every bookkeeping and claim write
Card-feature downgrade ladder (extended authorization + multicapture down to nothing) because unapproved Connect accounts error instead of silently ignoring the request
The real expiry is read from the charge's capture_before with its provenance persisted — never a hardcoded 31 days, which is what let holds die silently while the DB still showed 'held'
deposit_hold_chain_expires_at is a cache and a placement-only floor, not the authority: the refresher recomputes the bound from the rental's LIVE end_date on every pass
The success write is a compare-and-set on 'processing' AND our own attempt_seq; zero rows updated means we no longer own the slot and our authorisation is the orphan
A transport rejection on the success write is ambiguous, so the row is re-read before treating a live authorisation as an orphan and cancelling it
When the record write fails AND the cancel fails, a live authorisation exists that no row points at — the ledger row is then its only trace and is written either way
deposit_hold_target_amount is deliberately left NULL: two amount columns with no defined precedence will drift on a money path, so it is wired up together with its reader or not at all
Connect account, Stripe mode and currency of the hold are anchored on the rental so refresh/capture/release survive a UK->UAE platform flip mid-rental
Card brand/last4/expiry/funding are captured off the PaymentMethod so a 90-day chain is auditable and debit stacking is detectable without a Stripe round-trip per rental
Per-rental 'verdict' email to the super admin summarising whether the tenant's integrations were live-ready at the moment the rental was created
Fired by an AFTER INSERT trigger on public.rentals via pg_net — one alert per rental creation across every tenant
verify_jwt = false; the internal caller proves itself with an x-platform-secret header verified through the platform_verify_secret() RPC
The integration block is rendered from rentals.creation_context — a frozen snapshot of Stripe/BoldSign/Bonzah/subscription readiness at creation, not live configuration
rentals.health_severity (ok/warning/critical) drives the banner colour, subject-line emoji and the 'why this needs your eyes' block
Two-step in-house identity verification: OCR extraction then face match, with one verdict written back to identity_verifications
isMatch / needsReview / no-match map to verified / review_required / rejected and to Veriff-shaped GREEN / RETRY / RED review results
Additional-driver sessions carry customer_id NULL and external_user_id 'additional_driver_<uuid>', so the verdict is routed to rental_additional_drivers instead of customers
A post-verdict blocked_identities lookup can override a GREEN result to rejected and flag the customer as blocked
qr_session_token is nulled on completion so the mobile capture link cannot be replayed
OCR licence number and date of birth are copied onto the customer record alongside the verification status
Twilio recordingStatusCallback pipeline: download the MP3, transcribe with Whisper, summarise with GPT into action items, save to call_logs
The recording is downloaded with the TENANT's own Twilio credentials read off the tenants row, not a platform account
The MP3 is re-hosted in the 'voicemails' storage bucket so the browser can play it without Twilio auth
Every failure step still persists what it has (the raw Twilio URL, '[Transcription failed]') and returns 200 so Twilio does not retry the callback
Whisper is priced per minute, so its cost is logged with an explicit costOverride rather than token counts
The matching voice chat_channel_messages row is flagged has_transcript so the chat UI can offer the transcript
Hourly cron that charges the CUMULATIVE outstanding across every open past-due installment on a plan in a single off-session PaymentIntent
A 24h cooldown anchored on installment_plans.last_reminder_sent_at gates both charging and reminding (PAYG-style cadence)
Three consecutive SCA-required (authentication_required) failures flip the plan from auto to manual collection; non-SCA failures reset the counter

installment_plans has no platform_account column, so the saved card is anchored via the EARLIEST Stripe payment on the rental — charging with the current model after a UK->UAE flip throws 'No such customer'
A plan in auto mode with no saved card is flipped to manual and logged rather than retried forever
An optional only_rental_id hard-restricts a manual dispatch to one rental's plans so it can never charge another tenant
Every auto-charge outcome (succeeded / failed / skipped-no-card) is written to installment_notifications as an audit event
Poll Stripe for a checkout session and commit the payment when the webhook never arrived — the booking-success page's and rental detail page's safety net
A category-targeted payment that does not include 'Rental' must never settle an installment slot — settling with a Tax payment is the root cause of 'Tax: Not Paid but Collected = Tax amount'
Already-settled payments still run the installment lookup-and-settle, so revisiting the success page retroactively closes a slot left open by an older code path
rentalId is returned even on the alreadyProcessed branch so the booking-success page can still call place-deposit-hold when the webhook beat it to the row (R-b631e8)
The status UPDATE error is now checked: three separate constraint failures used to roll it back silently while the UI reported 'Payment Received' on a row still Pending
When the payment funded a rental extension, finalize_rental_extension atomically updates the extension, extends end_date without shrinking it, clears the legacy flags and back-stamps extension_id
Plan activation captures the saved payment method off the PaymentIntent and sets collection_mode to auto or manual accordingly, mirroring the webhook path
The LATEST overdue open slot is chosen because installment_settle_invoice cumulatively supersedes earlier ones, giving PAYG-style behaviour
Per-category refund (Rental / Tax / Service Fee / Security Deposit / Extension) validated against what that category was actually paid, minus what has already been refunded
Extension-category refunds MUST carry an extensionId or they orphan ledger rows and leave a payment status un-updated; a stale cached client bundle is the usual cause, so it fails loudly
Stripe's amount_refunded is the authority for what is still refundable — the local payments.refund_amount drifts after manual refunds, mixed payments and earlier failures
When Stripe has less room than requested, refund exactly what Stripe allows and record the remainder as a manual refund with a reconciliation note
The payment to refund is found through payment_applications on that category's charges, not the most recent Stripe payment on the rental (which could be an unrelated deposit capture)
The refund is distributed across EVERY contributing payment in most-applied-first order, so manual payments also flip off 'Paid' rather than only the Stripe-backed one
The Stripe block already synced refund_amount for its own payment; re-adding the allocation caused the $1.22 charge -> $2.44 refund_amount bug

capture_status is deliberately never written on refund — its CHECK constraint allows only requires_capture/captured/cancelled/expired/NULL; refund state lives on status + refund_amount + refund_processed_at
Two refunds on the same category on the same day collide on the unique index (rental_id, due_date, type, category, extension_id), so they are merged into the existing Refund row
Overdue-charge reminder cadence: Upcoming at T-2 days, Due at T-0, then Overdue at exactly 1, 7, 14, 21 and 28 days past due
A charge fully covered by the customer's credit balance is skipped when respect_credit_coverage is enabled
Every stage is independently switchable through reminder_settings key/value rows, including a max_overdue_reminders ceiling
Duplicate-key errors when inserting reminder_events are swallowed — the unique constraint IS the idempotency mechanism for a re-run
Reminders are only recorded as 'Delivered' with a message preview; the copy itself says the customer will be notified 'once channels are connected'
One endpoint serves two jobs: an immediate single refund when a paymentId is posted, and the batch of scheduled refunds due today when the body is empty
Refund ledger entries are split across Rental / Tax / Service Fee / Security Deposit in proportion to the latest invoice breakdown
Each refund is created with the keys and connected account of the platform the payment was CREATED on (payments.platform_account), never the tenant's current model
Fatal errors return HTTP 200 with success:false so the supabase-js caller does not see a FunctionsHttpError
A failed batch refund stamps refund_status='failed' and appends the error onto refund_reason so the row is not silently retried as pending
One-shot full RAG indexing of every indexed table for one tenant or every active tenant, populating rag_documents
knowledge_articles are indexed per tenant AND globally (tenant_id IS NULL) — the only table whose rows are shared across tenants
Documents are rendered with the tenant's currency_code so the embedded text carries the right money symbols
rag_documents is upserted on (tenant_id, source_table, source_id) so re-running the indexer replaces rather than duplicates
Incremental embedding refresh driven by rag_sync_queue rows that DB triggers enqueue on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
DELETE queue actions remove the rag_documents row, and a PGRST116 'record gone' on a re-read is treated the same way
A failed item is still stamped processed_at with an error_message, so one poisonous row cannot block the queue head forever
Tenant currency is cached per run so a 100-item queue does not perform 100 tenant lookups
Six-hourly sweep reconciling every non-terminal deposit hold in the database against the truth at Stripe
Nothing else in the codebase reads Stripe back: a deposit hold's PaymentIntent lives on rentals, has no payments row, and no webhook looks it up — so an expired authorisation shows 'Held' forever

Principle 1: read the hold with the platform account, connected account and mode it was CREATED under — the wrong platform's keys make Stripe report the PI missing, which looks exactly like an expired hold

Principle 2: an inconclusive read changes nothing, and a 'held' row is NEVER demoted, because every downstream guard keys on the literal 'held' — demoting would unblock a second authorisation and stop the release path at once
Principle 3: deposit_hold_expires_at is written only from a real capture_before; a moving now+7d fallback would re-arm the clock every 6 hours and the rental could never enter the refresh window

It never inserts a payments row, not even for a hold Stripe reports captured — backfilling payments keyed on a deposit-hold PaymentIntent arms the rental-cancellation path on every rental it touches (EC-23)
It touches money only to cancel a provably orphaned authorisation; cancelling releases a renter's funds and can never take them
verify_jwt=false, so the in-file check is the only gate: x-platform-secret (pg_cron) or a super-admin user JWT, and every error path fails closed
The service-role bearer is deliberately no longer accepted: a valid production service_role JWT is committed in plaintext in a migration and is pending rotation
net.http_post is asynchronous, so a 401 lands in net._http_response and never in cron.job_run_details — a schedule sending the wrong credential looks perfectly healthy while nothing is reconciled
The only thing that reaps rows stranded in a claim state (processing / refreshing / capturing) by a crash, a timeout or a deploy mid-flight — states invisible to every other code path

A deposit_hold_links row written for the rental in the last 30 minutes is a stronger liveness signal than deposit_hold_status_changed_at, which is NULL on exactly the legacy rows most in need of recovery
Compare-and-set on BOTH the status read and the PaymentIntent probed: the refresh engine can cancel PI_A, install a live PI_B and restore 'held' between the read and the write
resource_missing is INCONCLUSIVE (the anchor may be wrong, not the hold), so it is recorded in deposit_hold_last_error_code and only stranded claim states are demoted to needs_review
A cancelled PaymentIntent is resolved to 'released' when a human asked (release_requested_at, or cancellation_reason requested_by_customer) rather than recorded as a silent network expiry

A card-gone hold is handed back to the placement engine with a retry time, but deposit_hold_failure_count is deliberately NOT bumped — a reconciler seeing the same failure four times a day would compound the backoff into silence
Sweep A: a deposit_hold_links row still 'pending' an hour on belongs to a writer that died, and its PaymentIntent may be holding a renter's funds with nothing pointing at it
Sweep B: a superseded PaymentIntent still at requires_capture means the refresh engine's cancel failed and the renter is carrying two live holds
Keyset pagination everywhere: this pass writes statuses that remove rows from the filter it pages over, and the orphans that matter are the OLD ones a DESC-limit query would never reach

'Already checked' is recorded as ledger rows (orphan_cancel / reconcile:superseded_clear) rather than a new column because this workstream writes no DDL — and those actions are excluded from the candidate query so the sweep does not rediscover its own bookkeeping
loadRental and loadTenant THROW instead of returning undefined: a discarded read error would make the 'is this the rental's current hold?' comparison false and cancel a LIVE authorisation
Separate wall-clock reserves per sweep so a long pending-link pass cannot starve the superseded pass — they used to share one deadline and whichever ran second always lost
A cron_runs heartbeat row is written before any work, and scoped or dry runs are recorded under a DIFFERENT job_name so they cannot satisfy a dead-man alert meant for the real schedule
Truncation means 'we stopped before the query was exhausted' — deliberately not examined < totalDue, which would cry wolf on a healthy pass and train everyone to ignore the alert
closeLink returns whether the write actually landed: supabase-js resolves on a failed statement, so a bare await followed by a counter increment reports a failure as a resolution
The 35-day superseded lookback is a network FACT, not an optimistic assumption: no card authorisation outlives 30 days on any network (Visa 29d18h)

The authorisation's real currency is anchored from Stripe because currency is re-read from the CURRENT tenant row in three places, so a UK->UAE flip mid-rental can mint a replacement hold in a new currency (EC-45)
Safety net that materialises customers for renters who passed identity verification (GREEN) but never clicked 'Complete Registration', so the operator never saw them

MIN_AGE is 8 days — deliberately BEYOND the 7-day invite TTL — so a reconcile-created customer can never collide with a renter still self-completing and permanently block them with 'email already exists'
customers.email is unique PER TENANT, so the dedup match must be tenant-scoped, case-insensitive, and LIKE-escaped for '_' and '%' in the local part
Global blacklist, blocked-email and blocked-document guards are mirrored from submit-customer-registration so a blocked identity is never materialised
Creates data only — no email, SMS or webhook — and back-links the verification to the new customer, which is also the idempotency mechanism
Concrete incident: Flow Auto Rentals' 'Mary J Davis' passed verification, never completed registration, and had to be added by hand
Stripe is the authority and the DB is a cache: a webhook is a delivery guarantee, not a consistency guarantee, so anything missed while the endpoint was down stays wrong forever
Safety invariant 1: dry run BY DEFAULT — you must pass {"dryRun": false} for this function to write anything

Safety invariant 2: it writes ONLY tenant_subscriptions and never tenants.stripe_mode / bonzah_mode — replaying historic subscriptions through the webhook path would switch tenants to live Stripe Connect and live insurance
Safety invariant 3: a Stripe subscription that cannot be resolved to a tenant is reported as an orphan, never guessed at

The production incident this exists for: handleSubscriptionUpdated threw RangeError on every customer.subscription.updated after Stripe moved current_period_* onto items, and the status CHECK rejected 'incomplete_expired'
resolvePeriod reads current_period_* from the subscription AND from its first item, because Stripe's basil release relocated those fields

Never items.data[0]: subscriptions carry a metered e-sign price and a $1 card-verification line, so the headline amount is the LARGEST licensed unit_amount x quantity — reading [0] once rewrote a $350/mo plan as $1/mo
The card Stripe actually charges is looked up beyond subscription.default_payment_method — reading only that field left 19 of 26 live subscriptions showing 'No payment method on file'
Legacy Sources/Card API customers bill a customer default_source that paymentMethods.list never returns — several of the longest-standing paying tenants are on that path
Tenant resolution ordered most- to least-authoritative: Stripe metadata, an existing row by subscription id, by customer id, then tenants.stripe_subscription_customer_id
Stripe subscriptions outlive tenants: a metadata tenant_id pointing at a deleted row is reported as an orphan rather than failing the whole run on an FK error
A UAE-migrated tenant's legacy UK subscription is deliberately left alone — writing Stripe's UK view would trip the one-active-row partial index or show the old UK amount as current
Invoice-level reconciliation, because the portal's 7-day grace clock is anchored on the oldest LOCAL open invoice — a lost invoice.paid hard-paywalls a tenant Stripe already considers settled
Stripe rotates a token on invoice PDF and hosted URLs, so those links are FILLED when missing but never compared or rewritten — comparing them reported 29 of 29 invoices as drifted
attempt_count is the ONLY thing separating a declined invoice from one not yet due — the admin dashboard's red 'Payment failed' vs amber 'Unpaid' badge keys purely on it
Every column in INVOICE_COMPARED must appear in the select, or it reads back undefined and the row reports phantom drift on every run forever
The subscription row is adopted BEFORE its invoices, or invoices land with subscription_id NULL, the portal discards them, and a past_due tenant is neither warned nor blocked nor given a pay link
Invoices are reconciled before the 'subscription already in sync -> continue' short-circuit, because a stale invoice is what actually paywalls a tenant that otherwise looks fine
Never overwrite a good stored amount, card or billing period with a null or an unresolvable zero
This function had NO authorisation check: Supabase's default verify_jwt accepts the public anon key that ships in every browser bundle, and the response body is a cross-tenant dump
Four-cell uk/uae x test/live subscription account grid, with a missing key reported explicitly because a silently skipped account is exactly how drift hides
Record a payment the operator made to the issuing authority for a traffic fine
A P&L Cost entry under category 'Fines' is created with reference 'authority:<paymentId>' used as the idempotency key
A failed P&L write (including a duplicate-key replay) is logged but never fails the authority payment itself
Per-minute cron that scans recent Pending Stripe-attached payments, asks Stripe whether the session paid, and commits anything that did

Root cause it defends against: test-mode events arriving at stripe-webhook-live fail signature verification with a 400, leaving the payment Pending forever unless the customer redirects to a working app
Setting status='Completed' fires auto_fifo_on_payment_completed -> payment_apply_fifo_v2 -> auto_settle_payg_on_ledger_drain; the RPC is also called explicitly belt-and-braces

Pass 2 re-runs FIFO on CAPTURED payments stranded as status='Credit' with $0 allocated — payment_apply_fifo_v2 used to refuse to let an untagged payment settle Extension* charges (GMT, rental R-63b168)
Pass 2 heals only when the rental genuinely still has open charges, so a legitimate overpayment credit is never disturbed
refresh-deposit-holds: chain security-deposit authorizations across a long rental by cancelling each one before it expires and placing a replacement on the saved card

A single card authorization can never exceed ~30 days (Visa 29d18h; accounts without extended authorization get ~5-7), so a 90-120 day rental needs 4-18 links and the reliability of each link is the whole engineering problem
This file is only the DRIVER — which rentals are due, in what order, how many per run, and the heartbeat; every per-rental decision lives in _shared/deposit-hold-refresh.ts
The engine was extracted because sandbox-refresh-deposit-holds and this file were hand-maintained verbatim forks, so the Time Machine was green-lighting logic production no longer ran
A .lt() against a NULL deposit_hold_expires_at yields NULL rather than true, so rows with no known expiry were invisible to the old due filter

'failed' rows are retried only when they evidence a real prior authorization (a PaymentIntent or a placed_at stamp) — the Stripe webhooks write the same status when the FIRST placement never succeeded, and those rows are not this engine's to touch
Rental lifecycle is a terminal-status DENY list rather than an ('Active','Pending') allow list, so a status nobody enumerated cannot silently end a chain
Oldest deadline first with NULLs first (unsecured rentals), a bounded batch and a 240s wall-clock budget so nothing is killed mid-Stripe-call with a row parked in 'refreshing'

A refresh is DESTRUCTIVE — it cancels the live authorisation before placing its replacement — so an unauthenticated caller who merely knew a rental UUID could force a cancel-and-reauthorize; the gate accepts only the platform secret or a super-admin JWT
config_unavailable is kept OUT of `failed` (one mis-configured tenant would erode the dead-man signal) but is still a silent death, so it raises one aggregated, day-deduped bell per tenant
The engine's contract is to return rather than throw; a throw means nothing wrote a status and the row is left wherever the throw interrupted it, so the alert claims moneyState 'unknown'
Rows stuck in 'refreshing' for over an hour are counted and surfaced but deliberately NOT reaped — deciding whether their authorization exists requires probing Stripe, which belongs to the reconciler
Refund every PAID installment plus the plan's upfront payment, then cancel the plan, when a booking with an installment plan is rejected or cancelled
resolveForRecord pins each refund's Stripe client and connected account to the platform the linked PAYMENT was created on, never the tenant's current model
A Stripe charge_already_refunded error is counted as a successful refund rather than an error
Refund ledger entries are split by category from payment_applications, falling back to the invoice breakdown (deposit, service fee, tax, delivery, then Rental), then to a single Rental entry
Installments marked paid manually carry no Stripe PaymentIntent, so nothing is refunded on Stripe and the operator handles them
cancel_installment_plan closes the plan and cancels its remaining scheduled installments after the money has been returned
Reject a booking end to end: refund or release every active payment, write Refund ledger entries, cancel the rental, release the vehicle and cancel unpaid charges
A requires_capture payment is CANCELLED (the hold is released); a captured one is refunded — resolved per payment from capture_status
A missing stripe_payment_intent_id is resolved from the checkout session and written back onto the payment for future reference
Payments with no Stripe PaymentIntent are marked refund_status='pending_manual' rather than silently dropped
payment_applications, payment ledger entries and charge remaining_amounts are deliberately left INTACT and Refund entries added on top, so the UI still shows what was paid as well as refunded
P&L revenue entries whose source_ref starts with the refunded payment id are deleted, so a rejected booking stops counting as revenue

hyperedges.label: Deposit-hold authorisation lifecycle: claim, authorise, ledger, chain, reconcile, reap
The five independent paths that can settle an installment slot
Every webhook in this system has a polling or sweep counterpart, because deliveries drop
